title: Hardening of the Heart
lead: The Bible's language for a will set against God, most famously Pharaoh's in Exodus 4–14, where God and Pharaoh both are said to harden it. Paul takes it up in Romans 9, and the theme returns in the Psalms, the prophets and the Gospels (Psalm 95:8; Isaiah 6:10; Mark 6:52).

sections.b: The language of a hardened heart returns often. God hardens the spirit of King Sihon (Deuteronomy 2:30) and the Canaanite kings (Joshua 11:20). The Philistine priests warn their people not to make their hearts heavy "the way Egypt and Pharaoh made their hearts heavy" (1 Samuel 6:6). Isaiah is sent to make the people's heart dull (Isaiah 6:10), and later the people ask why God has let their hearts grow hard (Isaiah 63:17). Psalm 95:8 warns, "Do not make your hearts hard, as at Meribah."
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 2:30; Joshua 11:20; 1 Samuel 6:6; Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 63:17; Psalm 95:8

sections.b: The Gospels quote Isaiah 6:10 to explain unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40), and Mark says even the disciples' hearts were hardened (Mark 6:52; 8:17). Paul uses Pharaoh as his example in Romans 9:17–18 and speaks of a partial hardening on Israel "until the nations have come in to their full number" (Romans 11:7, 25). Hebrews applies Psalm 95 to believers: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not make your hearts hard" (Hebrews 3:7–15).
sections.refs: Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40; Mark 6:52; Mark 8:17; Romans 9:17–18; Romans 11:7; Romans 11:25; Hebrews 3:7–15
